scenes.title: Amazon Comprehend
scenes.narration: Amazon Comprehend analyses text to extract useful signals for routing and organization. Read the example customer email on the far left: the sender says they cannot log in and needs help. Follow the numbered steps across the diagram. First, language detection identifies the language. Second, key-phrase extraction finds expressions such as login and account. Third, sentiment analysis estimates how positive or negative the wording is, including a score. Fourth, topic detection and related text labels help describe the issue, for example account access or technical support. The rightmost branch shows what the application can do with these results: route a ticket, add searchable tags, and save structured information. The bottom reminder is important. Comprehend is a natural-language analysis service; it does not itself generate a long conversational answer like a foundation model. Use the extracted labels as inputs to workflows, with confidence checks and human escalation where needed.

scenes.title: Custom Document Classification
scenes.narration: This slide explains when predefined Comprehend analysis is not enough. On the left are example training documents already labelled billing, access and complaint. Those labels belong to the business's own ticket taxonomy. Follow them into the Amazon Comprehend custom classifier in the centre. The classifier learns to recognise patterns that distinguish those classes. Now a new customer email arrives, asking about a charged device and an order. On the right, the classifier assigns a label and the application uses it to route the request to the appropriate team. The lower part of the image compares two ways to analyse documents: synchronous processing of an individual document for quick results, and asynchronous batch processing for a larger collection stored in S3. Choose based on the application latency and throughput needs. Most importantly, the training labels must be consistent and representative; otherwise the classifier can confidently automate the wrong routing decision.

scenes.title: Named Entity Recognition
scenes.narration: Named Entity Recognition, or NER, converts important mentions in text into structured fields. The sentence at the top says that Sarah Johnson visited Seattle to meet Amazon on March twelfth, twenty twenty-four. Follow the colour highlights. Sarah Johnson is classified as a person, Seattle as a location, Amazon as an organization, and the date as a date. The lower-left table turns the coloured mentions into extracted entities that software can work with. The neighbouring panel shows the original sentence with the same spans visually highlighted, reminding us that entities are identified in the context of actual text. This differs from simply looking for a fixed list of words: classification depends on how the term is used. Generic NER can recognize common categories, but your business may also need specialized identifiers. In the next slide, we'll teach a model to find those domain-specific mentions.

scenes.title: Custom Entity Recognition
scenes.narration: Now the slide introduces domain-specific entities that a general NER model may not understand. Start with the annotated support-message examples on the left. They highlight a policy number and a phrase requesting escalation to the executive team. In the middle, those labelled examples train a custom entity recognizer. The recognizer is then applied to a new message shown on the right. Notice how the extracted policy number and escalation phrase become structured fields rather than disappearing in the surrounding prose. The bottom-left comparison contrasts generic NER categories such as person or location with custom business labels such as POLICY_NUMBER and ESCALATION_PHRASE. The two lower-right execution paths illustrate synchronous analysis of an individual record and asynchronous analysis of many records. A good custom recognizer needs carefully labelled training examples, testing against unfamiliar documents, and permission controls over sensitive inputs and outputs.

scenes.title: Comprehend and Lambda Data Quality
scenes.narration: This is a multi-service data-quality workflow. Follow the main row: incoming documents, user text, or application data first reach AWS Lambda. Lambda calls Amazon Comprehend to detect language, identify PII, extract entities, or classify the text according to the configured operation. Those results lead to an approved structured-text stage, where the application can redact sensitive findings or apply business validation rules. Only after review and handling do the approved results move toward Amazon Bedrock for later generation or a Knowledge Base for structured retrieval. Look at the red sensitive-findings branch underneath. If the analysis identifies personal or sensitive content, an authorized reviewer can decide whether to mask, remove, or reject it. The purple warning along the bottom is essential: Comprehend can help detect PII, but its predictions do not guarantee complete removal of every sensitive detail. Security and compliance require additional controls and testing.

scenes.title: Amazon Comprehend Medical
scenes.narration: Our final text-analysis example involves a clinical note. On the left, the note mentions medicines, conditions and medical procedures. The middle block uses Amazon Comprehend Medical to extract clinically relevant entity types from that unstructured language. Look at the right-hand outputs: a medication such as lisinopril, a condition such as hypertension, and a procedure such as knee replacement. A separate protected-health-information branch concerns detecting personal health identifiers, including names, dates and contact details where supported. These tasks are related but not identical, and identifying PHI is not automatically the same as securely de-identifying every record. The bottom banner calls for strong access controls and privacy review. Restrict who can send and view clinical material, monitor usage, and have qualified staff review critical results. This wraps up Comprehend's role: turning text into meaningful structured signals for downstream applications without treating predicted labels as infallible.
